property_summary: After a first call sends 10 ether at time t, a second call also sending 10 ether at the same timestamp t should revert on the reference (requiring strictly greater) but succeeds on the modified version (requiring greater or equal).

Two calls before any state change: in the reference, block.timestamp must be strictly greater than pastBlockTime; in the bug, it can be equal. By calling fallback() twice with the same block timestamp and 10 ether each, the reference reverts the second call due to require(block.timestamp > pastBlockTime) failing, whereas the buggy version accepts it and then transfers the balance when block.number % 15 == 0.

After a call that sets pastBlockTime, calling fallback with 10 ether at the same block timestamp reverts in the reference (strict >) but succeeds in the modified version (>=), causing balance to increase in the buggy version.
After a call that sets pastBlockTime to t, a subsequent call at the same timestamp t with 10 ether should revert in the reference (requiring >) but passes in the buggy version (requiring >=).

After a first call to fallback at block.number % 15 == 0 (sending 10 ether), a second call with exactly the same timestamp causes the reference to revert (require strict >) but the buggy version to accept (require >=), allowing repeated withdrawal of the entire contract balance.

After a successful fallback call that satisfies the time check and block condition, the reference version updates pastBlockTime while the second version does not, so a subsequent call with the same block.timestamp will revert in the reference but succeed in the second version.

Two consecutive calls to the fallback function with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp increasing should both succeed in the reference version, but the buggy version omits updating pastBlockTime, causing the second call to revert due to the time check failing.

After a fallback call with 10 ether at a block where block.number % 15 != 0, the reference sets pastBlockTime to block.timestamp, while the buggy version does not, causing a subsequent call at the same timestamp to revert in the reference but succeed in the buggy version.

After two identical 10-ether fallback calls from the same sender at block numbers where mode 15 changes, the reference contract transfers no balance on the second call (block % 15 != 0), leaving contract balance at 20 ether, while the buggy version transfers 10 ether on the second call (block % 15 == 0) and thus contract balance is 10 ether.

After a first call that sets pastBlockTime and triggers the transfer because block.number % 15 == 0, a second call with the same sender, same value, and a later timestamp correctly reverts in the reference (require(block.timestamp > pastBlockTime) fails) but sends the entire balance to the caller in the buggy version (because the if condition is != 0, so the transfer executes even when the timestamp check should fail).
After a first call sends 10 ether and block.number % 15 == 0, the reference transfers the entire contract balance to the caller; the buggy version does not transfer because the condition uses != 0.

After a fallback call with 10 ether at a block number where block.number % 15 == 0, the reference version sends the entire contract balance to msg.sender, while the buggy version does not, so after an initial call at such a block and a second call at a block where block.number % 15 != 0, the contract balance is zero in the reference but positive in the buggy version.
After a call meeting the condition (10 ETH, block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, block.number % 15 != 0), the reference does not transfer balance, while the bug does, making address(c).balance differ.

After two identical fallback calls with 10 ether each in the same block, the reference contract only transfers balance back if block.number % 15 == 0, while the buggy contract always transfers, causing address(c).balance to be 0 after the second call in the buggy version.

After first call to fallback with 10 ether, when block.number%15==0, the reference transfers all balance to msg.sender; the buggy version always transfers, so after second call at a block where block.number%15 != 0, the reference retains balance while the buggy version sends it away.

After a successful fallback call at a block number that is NOT a multiple of 15, the reference contract keeps its balance (does not transfer), while the buggy contract transfers all balance to the caller.

After two calls to fallback() with 10 ether each, the first at a block where block.number % 15 == 0 (reference transfers balance, bug always transfers), then observing c's balance after the second call: reference has 10 ether remaining because it transferred in the first call, bug has 0 ether because it transferred again in the second call.

After two identical fallback calls that succeed, the reference contract resets the condition block.number % 15 == 0 only every 15 blocks, while the buggy version with if(true) always sends the entire balance to msg.sender; the concrete scenario uses block number 1 (not multiple of 15) and after first call the balance is 10 ether, the second call should NOT send the balance in the reference (balance stays 10) but does send it in the buggy version (balance becomes 0).
